widgets.title: SN1 mechanism, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1 (slow, rate-determining): the C–X bond ionises, giving a planar carbocation and X⁻. Rate = k[R–X].;;Step 2: the carbocation is sp² with an empty p-orbital, so the nucleophile can attack either face.;;Step 3 (fast): Nu attacks the carbocation to give the substitution product; a stereogenic carbon gives a mixture of both configurations.;;Note: a 1,2-hydride or alkyl shift can occur before attack if it gives a more stable carbocation.

widgets.title: SN1 energy profile (two steps)
widgets.note: Schematic profile: heights are illustrative, not measured values.

widgets.title: SN2 mechanism, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the nucleophile (Nu⁻) approaches the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group (backside attack, about 180° to the C–X bond).;;Step 2: a single transition state forms: Nu and X are both partly bonded to a planar, five-coordinate carbon; the other three groups lie in a plane.;;Step 3: in the same step the C–X bond breaks as the C–Nu bond forms; the leaving group departs with the bonding pair.;;Result: the configuration at carbon is inverted (Walden inversion). Rate = k[R–X][Nu⁻].

widgets.title: SN2 energy profile (one step)
widgets.note: Schematic profile: heights are illustrative, not measured values.

widgets.title: E2 mechanism, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: a strong base approaches a β-hydrogen that is anti-periplanar to the leaving group.;;Step 2: in one concerted step the C–H bond breaks, the C=C π bond forms and the leaving group departs.;;Result: rate = k[R–X][Base]. The more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene is usually the major product; a bulky base can favour the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene.

widgets.title: E1 mechanism, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1 (slow): the leaving group departs, giving a carbocation (the same first step as SN1). Rate = k[R–X].;;Step 2 (fast): a weak base removes a β-hydrogen from a carbon next to the cationic carbon.;;Result: the C=C bond forms; the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene usually predominates. Rearrangement of the carbocation is possible.

widgets.title: Nucleophilic addition to C=O, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon at about 107° to the C=O axis (Bürgi–Dunitz angle), interacting with the C=O π* orbital (the LUMO).;;Step 2: the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate; the carbon changes from sp² to sp³.;;Step 3: protonation of the alkoxide (by acid or solvent) gives the addition product.;;Reactivity: aldehydes react faster than ketones because the carbonyl carbon is less hindered and more electrophilic.

widgets.title: Base-catalysed aldol reaction, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: a base removes an α-hydrogen from one carbonyl compound, forming an enolate.;;Step 2: the enolate carbon attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule, forming a new C–C bond and an alkoxide.;;Step 3: protonation of the alkoxide gives the β-hydroxy carbonyl compound (the aldol).;;Step 4: on heating, loss of water (E1cB) gives the α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound.

title: ^7\. Electrophilic aromatic substitution: the general mechanism

widgets.title: Electrophilic aromatic substitution, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the electrophile E⁺ is generated (for nitration, NO₂⁺ from HNO₃ and H₂SO₄).;;Step 2 (slow, rate-determining): the π system of benzene attacks E⁺, giving a resonance-stabilised arenium ion (σ-complex); aromaticity is temporarily lost.;;Step 3 (fast): a base removes H⁺ from the sp³ carbon, restoring aromaticity and giving the substituted benzene.

widgets.title: EAS energy profile (two steps)
widgets.note: Schematic profile: heights are illustrative, not measured values.

widgets.title: 1,2-hydride shift in a carbocation
widgets.steps: Start: a secondary carbocation is next to a carbon that carries a hydrogen and is more substituted.;;Step 1: the hydrogen moves with its bonding pair to the cationic carbon (1,2-hydride shift).;;Result: the positive charge is now on the more substituted carbon, giving a more stable (tertiary) carbocation.

widgets.title: Free-radical chlorination of an alkane, step by step
widgets.steps: Initiation: UV light or heat splits Cl–Cl homolytically: Cl₂ → 2 Cl•.;;Propagation 1: a chlorine atom abstracts a hydrogen from the alkane: R–H + Cl• → R• + HCl.;;Propagation 2: the alkyl radical takes a chlorine atom from Cl₂: R• + Cl₂ → R–Cl + Cl•. The chlorine atom is regenerated, so the chain continues.;;Termination: two radicals combine (Cl• + Cl•, R• + Cl•, R• + R•), which removes radicals and ends the chain.;;Selectivity: weaker C–H bonds react faster (3° > 2° > 1°); bromine is much more selective than chlorine.

title: ^18\. Electrophilic addition to alkenes: the general picture

widgets.title: Electrophilic addition of HBr to propene (Markovnikov), step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the π electrons of the alkene attack the electrophilic hydrogen of H–Br, and H–Br breaks heterolytically.;;Step 2: hydrogen adds to the carbon that gives the more stable carbocation. For propene, H adds to CH₂, giving a secondary carbocation.;;Step 3: bromide ion attacks the carbocation, giving 2-bromopropane (the Markovnikov product).;;Note: if a 1,2-hydride or alkyl shift can give a more stable carbocation, rearranged products form.

widgets.title: Peroxide effect: radical addition of HBr to propene, step by step
widgets.steps: Initiation: a peroxide splits into alkoxy radicals, and RO• takes a hydrogen from HBr: RO• + HBr → ROH + Br•.;;Step 1: the bromine atom adds to the less substituted carbon of the alkene, giving the more stable (secondary) carbon radical.;;Step 2: the carbon radical takes a hydrogen from HBr, giving the product and regenerating Br•, so the chain continues.;;Result: the anti-Markovnikov product, 1-bromopropane. Under ordinary conditions only HBr shows this peroxide effect.

widgets.title: Nucleophilic acyl substitution (addition–elimination), step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1 (addition): the nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon, the C=O π bond breaks, and a tetrahedral intermediate forms.;;Step 2 (elimination): the C=O re-forms and the leaving group is expelled (Cl⁻ from an acyl chloride, RCOO⁻ from an anhydride, RO⁻ from an ester).;;Reactivity order: acyl chloride > anhydride > ester ≈ carboxylic acid > amide, following leaving-group ability and resonance donation into the carbonyl.

widgets.title: Acid-catalysed dehydration of a secondary or tertiary alcohol (E1), step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the acid protonates the OH group, giving R–OH₂⁺, which has a good leaving group (H₂O).;;Step 2 (slow): water leaves, giving a carbocation.;;Step 3: a base (H₂O or HSO₄⁻) removes a β-hydrogen, forming the C=C bond. The more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene predominates.;;Notes: ease of dehydration is 3° > 2° > 1°, and the carbocation may rearrange before the alkene forms.

widgets.title: Hofmann bromamide degradation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: Br₂/NaOH converts the primary amide into the N-bromoamide, R–CO–NHBr.;;Step 2: base removes the N–H proton, giving the N-bromoamide anion.;;Step 3: the R group migrates from carbon to nitrogen as bromide leaves, forming an isocyanate, R–N=C=O. The migrating group keeps its configuration.;;Step 4: water adds to the isocyanate to give a carbamic acid, which loses CO₂ to give the primary amine R–NH₂, with one carbon fewer than the amide.

widgets.title: Pinacol–pinacolone rearrangement, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: acid protonates one OH group of the vicinal diol.;;Step 2: water leaves, giving a carbocation at the more stabilised carbon.;;Step 3: a group on the neighbouring carbinol carbon migrates to the cationic carbon (1,2-shift).;;Step 4: the oxygen lone pair stabilises the new cation as a protonated carbonyl; loss of H⁺ gives the ketone (pinacolone).

widgets.title: Beckmann rearrangement of an oxime, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: acid (or PCl₅ or TsCl) converts the oxime OH into a good leaving group.;;Step 2: the group anti to the leaving group migrates from carbon to nitrogen as the leaving group departs, giving a nitrilium ion.;;Step 3: water adds to the nitrilium carbon.;;Step 4: tautomerisation gives the N-substituted amide. For cyclohexanone oxime the product is caprolactam.

widgets.title: Free-radical chain polymerisation, step by step
widgets.steps: Initiation: an initiator such as a peroxide decomposes into radicals, and a radical adds to the C=C of a monomer to give a new radical.;;Propagation: the growing chain radical adds to another monomer, and this repeats many times.;;Termination: two chain radicals combine or disproportionate, which ends the chain.;;Chain transfer to another molecule can stop one chain and start another, lowering the molar mass.

widgets.title: Mutarotation of D-glucose, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: in water, the cyclic hemiacetal (α- or β-D-glucopyranose) opens to the free-chain aldehyde form, present in only a tiny amount.;;Step 2: the ring-closing oxygen (O-5) attacks the aldehyde carbon (C-1) from either face.;;Step 3: attack from one face gives the α anomer; from the other face, the β anomer.;;Result: the specific rotation drifts from +112° (pure α) or +18.7° (pure β) to a constant +52.7°, an equilibrium of about 36% α and 64% β.

widgets.title: Friedel–Crafts acylation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: AlCl₃ takes Cl⁻ from the acyl chloride, giving the acylium ion R–C≡O⁺, which does not rearrange.;;Step 2: the arene π system attacks the acylium ion, giving the arenium (σ-complex) ion.;;Step 3: AlCl₄⁻ removes the ring proton, restoring aromaticity and giving the aryl ketone.;;Note: the ketone product complexes AlCl₃, so more than one equivalent of AlCl₃ is needed. The deactivated ring does not acylate a second time.

widgets.title: Wittig reaction, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: Ph₃P reacts with an alkyl halide (SN2) to give the phosphonium salt.;;Step 2: a strong base removes an α-hydrogen, giving the ylide Ph₃P⁺–C⁻R₂.;;Step 3: the ylide carbon attacks the carbonyl carbon, giving a betaine and then a four-membered oxaphosphetane.;;Step 4: the oxaphosphetane collapses to the alkene and Ph₃P=O. The strong P=O bond drives the reaction.

widgets.title: Grignard addition to a carbonyl, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: Mg inserts into the C–X bond of R–X in dry ether, giving R–MgX. The carbon is now strongly nucleophilic.;;Step 2: the R group attacks the carbonyl carbon and the C=O π bond breaks, giving a magnesium alkoxide.;;Step 3: aqueous acid (H₃O⁺) protonates the alkoxide.;;Result: formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol, other aldehydes give secondary alcohols, ketones give tertiary alcohols. Any acidic H (water, alcohol) destroys the reagent.

widgets.title: Cannizzaro reaction, step by step
widgets.steps: Condition: an aldehyde with no α-hydrogen, in concentrated NaOH.;;Step 1: OH⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon of one molecule, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide anion.;;Step 2: this anion transfers a hydride (H⁻) to the carbonyl carbon of a second aldehyde molecule.;;Step 3: the donor becomes the carboxylic acid (then its carboxylate salt) and the acceptor becomes the alkoxide, which is protonated to the alcohol.;;Result: one half is oxidised and the other half reduced (disproportionation).

widgets.title: Claisen condensation of ethyl acetate, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: ethoxide removes an α-hydrogen from the ester, giving an enolate. Only a small amount forms.;;Step 2: the enolate attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second ester molecule, giving a tetrahedral intermediate.;;Step 3: ethoxide is expelled, giving the β-keto ester.;;Step 4: the β-keto ester has very acidic α-hydrogens (between two C=O), so base removes one. This forms a stable enolate and drives the equilibrium forward, so a full equivalent of base is needed.;;Step 5: acid work-up gives the neutral β-keto ester.

widgets.title: Williamson ether synthesis, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: a strong base (Na or NaH) converts the alcohol or phenol to its alkoxide RO⁻.;;Step 2: the alkoxide attacks the alkyl halide by SN2, with backside attack and inversion at carbon.;;Step 3: the halide leaves, giving the ether R–O–R'.;;Limit: use a methyl or primary alkyl halide. Secondary halides give mostly elimination, and tertiary halides give only elimination (alkenes).

widgets.title: Ring opening of an epoxide, step by step
widgets.steps: Basic or nucleophilic conditions (RO⁻, RMgX, LiAlH₄): the nucleophile attacks the less hindered carbon by SN2, with inversion, relieving ring strain.;;The resulting alkoxide is protonated in the work-up to give the alcohol.;;Acidic conditions: the epoxide oxygen is protonated first, and the nucleophile attacks the carbon that better bears positive charge (the more substituted carbon).;;In both cases attack is from the face opposite the oxygen, so the product has trans (anti) stereochemistry.

widgets.title: Diazotisation of a primary aromatic amine, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: NaNO₂ + HCl at 0–5 °C gives nitrous acid, then the nitrosonium ion NO⁺.;;Step 2: the amine nitrogen attacks NO⁺, giving an N-nitrosoammonium ion; loss of H⁺ gives the N-nitrosoamine.;;Step 3: tautomerisation gives the diazohydroxide, Ar–N=N–OH.;;Step 4: protonation and loss of water give the arenediazonium ion, Ar–N₂⁺. It is stable only at low temperature (0–5 °C).

widgets.title: Azo coupling, step by step
widgets.steps: The diazonium ion is a weak electrophile, so it couples only with strongly activated rings (phenoxide, aniline).;;Step 1: the activated ring attacks the terminal nitrogen of Ar–N₂⁺, usually at the para position (ortho if para is blocked).;;Step 2: loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity, giving the azo compound Ar–N=N–Ar', which is coloured.;;pH: phenols couple in mildly alkaline solution (pH 9–10), amines in mildly acidic solution (pH 4–5).

widgets.title: Gabriel synthesis of a primary amine, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: base removes the acidic N–H of phthalimide, giving the phthalimide anion.;;Step 2: the anion attacks a primary alkyl halide by SN2, giving N-alkylphthalimide.;;Step 3: hydrazinolysis (or hydrolysis) cleaves the imide, releasing the primary amine R–NH₂ and phthalhydrazide.;;Result: a pure primary amine with no 2° or 3° amine contamination. It fails with aryl halides because they do not undergo SN2.

widgets.title: Hofmann elimination, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: exhaustive methylation with excess CH₃I converts the amine to a quaternary ammonium iodide.;;Step 2: Ag₂O/H₂O exchanges iodide for hydroxide, giving R₄N⁺ OH⁻.;;Step 3: on heating, OH⁻ removes a β-hydrogen in an E2 step while NMe₃ leaves.;;Regiochemistry: the bulky leaving group makes the least hindered β-hydrogen the one removed, so the least substituted alkene (Hofmann product) predominates.

widgets.title: SNAr on a nitro-activated aryl halide, step by step
widgets.steps: Requirement: a strong electron-withdrawing group (such as NO₂) ortho or para to the leaving group.;;Step 1 (slow): the nucleophile attacks the carbon bearing the halogen, giving a resonance-stabilised Meisenheimer complex. The negative charge is delocalised onto the nitro group.;;Step 2 (fast): the halide leaves and aromaticity is restored.;;Reactivity: the rate-determining step is attack, so F > Cl > Br > I, the opposite of SN2 leaving-group order.

widgets.title: Baeyer–Villiger oxidation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the peracid protonates the carbonyl oxygen, and its OOH group adds to the carbonyl carbon, giving the Criegee intermediate.;;Step 2: a group on carbon migrates to the adjacent oxygen as the carboxylate leaves.;;Migratory aptitude: tertiary > cyclohexyl ≈ secondary > phenyl > primary > methyl. The migrating group keeps its configuration.;;Result: a ketone becomes an ester, and a cyclic ketone becomes a lactone.

widgets.title: Diels–Alder reaction, step by step
widgets.steps: Reactants: a conjugated diene (4π electrons) and a dienophile (2π electrons), usually bearing an electron-withdrawing group.;;The diene must adopt the s-cis conformation.;;The reaction is a single concerted step: two new C–C σ bonds form and a new C=C forms, giving a cyclohexene.;;Stereochemistry: it is suprafacial on both partners, so the stereochemistry of the dienophile is kept in the product. The endo product usually predominates.

widgets.title: Birch reduction of benzene, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: sodium in liquid ammonia (with an alcohol) donates an electron to the arene, giving a radical anion.;;Step 2: the alcohol protonates the radical anion, giving a cyclohexadienyl radical.;;Step 3: a second electron gives a cyclohexadienyl anion, which is protonated again.;;Result: 1,4-cyclohexadiene. Electron-donating groups (such as OMe) end up on the remaining C=C; electron-withdrawing groups (such as COOH) end up on the sp³ carbons.

widgets.title: Haloform (iodoform) reaction, step by step
widgets.steps: Requirement: a methyl ketone, CH₃–CO–R (or an alcohol oxidised to one, such as ethanol or propan-2-ol).;;Step 1: base forms the enolate, which is halogenated at the α-carbon. This repeats until all three α-hydrogens are replaced, giving R–CO–CX₃.;;Step 2: OH⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon, and the CX₃⁻ group leaves because three halogens stabilise it.;;Step 3: proton transfer gives the carboxylate RCOO⁻ and the haloform CHX₃. With iodine, yellow CHI₃ precipitates (the iodoform test).

widgets.title: Michael (1,4-conjugate) addition, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: base removes a proton from the donor (such as a malonate or β-keto ester), giving a stabilised enolate.;;Step 2: the enolate attacks the β-carbon of the α,β-unsaturated carbonyl (the acceptor), giving a new enolate.;;Step 3: protonation of this enolate gives the 1,4-adduct.;;Soft nucleophiles (enolates, cuprates) prefer 1,4-addition; hard nucleophiles (RLi, RMgX) tend to give 1,2-addition.

widgets.title: Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction, step by step
widgets.steps: Requirement: a carboxylic acid with at least one α-hydrogen.;;Step 1: PBr₃ (or P + Br₂) converts the acid to the acyl bromide.;;Step 2: the acyl bromide enolises more easily than the acid, and Br₂ brominates the α-carbon.;;Step 3: water hydrolyses the α-bromo acyl bromide to the α-bromo carboxylic acid.

widgets.title: Reimer–Tiemann reaction, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: NaOH removes a proton from CHCl₃, which loses Cl⁻ to give dichlorocarbene, :CCl₂.;;Step 2: the electron-rich phenoxide ring attacks the electron-poor carbene at the ortho position, giving a dichloromethyl intermediate.;;Step 3: hydrolysis of the CHCl₂ group by hydroxide gives the aldehyde.;;Result: salicylaldehyde (o-hydroxybenzaldehyde) is the main product, with a little para isomer.

widgets.title: Hydroboration–oxidation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: BH₃ (as BH₃·THF) adds across the C=C in one concerted step. Boron goes to the less hindered carbon and hydrogen to the other, both on the same face (syn addition).;;Step 2: this repeats until a trialkylborane R₃B forms.;;Step 3: H₂O₂/NaOH replaces each C–B bond with C–OH, with retention of configuration.;;Result: syn, anti-Markovnikov addition of water. A terminal alkene gives the primary alcohol; there is no carbocation, so no rearrangement.

widgets.title: Oxymercuration–demercuration, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: Hg(OAc)₂ adds to the alkene, forming a cyclic mercurinium ion.;;Step 2: water attacks the more substituted carbon (the one bearing more positive charge) from the opposite face.;;Step 3: NaBH₄ replaces the C–Hg bond with C–H.;;Result: Markovnikov addition of water without carbocation rearrangement.

title: ^22\. Epoxidation and the two routes to diols

widgets.title: Epoxidation with a peracid, then ring opening to a diol
widgets.steps: Step 1: the alkene π bond attacks the electrophilic terminal oxygen of RCO₃H in a single concerted step (the 'butterfly' transition state).;;Step 2: the oxygen is delivered to one face, so a cis alkene gives a cis epoxide and a trans alkene a trans epoxide (syn addition).;;Route A: acid-catalysed hydrolysis opens the epoxide by backside attack, giving the anti (trans) diol.;;Route B: OsO₄ or cold alkaline KMnO₄ adds both OH groups to the same face, giving the syn (cis) diol.

widgets.title: Catalytic hydrogenation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: H₂ adsorbs on the metal surface (Pd, Pt or Ni) and the H–H bond breaks, giving metal-bound hydrogen atoms.;;Step 2: the alkene adsorbs on the surface through its π bond.;;Step 3: two hydrogen atoms transfer to the same face of the C=C, so the addition is syn.;;Step 4: the alkane desorbs. Less hindered alkenes react faster, and a heterogeneous catalyst does not reduce benzene under mild conditions.

widgets.title: Controlling alkyne reduction: cis, trans or full
widgets.steps: H₂ with Lindlar catalyst (poisoned Pd): syn addition of H₂ stops at the alkene, giving the cis (Z) alkene.;;Na or Li in liquid NH₃: an electron adds to the alkyne, giving a radical anion; it is protonated to a vinyl radical, then reduced and protonated again.;;The vinyl anion prefers the trans arrangement, so dissolving-metal reduction gives the trans (E) alkene.;;H₂ with ordinary Pd/C: the reaction does not stop at the alkene and gives the alkane.

widgets.title: Hydride reduction of a ketone, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the hydride donor (H⁻ from NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄) attacks the carbonyl carbon, breaking the C=O π bond to give an alkoxide.;;Step 2: protonation of the alkoxide (solvent for NaBH₄, or water/acid work-up for LiAlH₄) gives the alcohol.;;Result: an aldehyde gives a primary alcohol and a ketone a secondary alcohol.;;Selectivity: NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes and ketones only. LiAlH₄ also reduces esters, acids and amides, and reacts violently with water.

widgets.title: Chromic acid oxidation of a secondary alcohol, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the alcohol reacts with H₂CrO₄ to form a chromate ester, R₂CH–O–CrO₃H.;;Step 2: a base (water) removes the α-hydrogen while the O–Cr bond breaks, forming C=O and reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(IV). The orange solution turns green as Cr(III) forms.;;Result: a secondary alcohol gives a ketone; a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde, which aqueous chromic acid oxidises further to the acid.;;PCC in dry CH₂Cl₂ stops at the aldehyde. Tertiary alcohols have no α-hydrogen and are not oxidised.

widgets.title: Wolff–Kishner reduction, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the ketone condenses with hydrazine (NH₂NH₂) to give a hydrazone, C=N–NH₂.;;Step 2: base (KOH) removes an N–H proton and the carbon is protonated, giving a diazene anion.;;Step 3: loss of N₂ gives a carbanion, which is protonated by the solvent.;;Result: C=O becomes CH₂ under strongly basic conditions. Use it for acid-sensitive substrates.

widgets.title: Clemmensen reduction, in outline
widgets.steps: Reagent: zinc amalgam (Zn–Hg) and concentrated HCl, heated.;;The reaction takes place on the zinc surface; the exact mechanism is not fully settled.;;Result: C=O becomes CH₂ under strongly acidic conditions. Use it for base-sensitive substrates.;;Choose by sensitivity: Clemmensen for acid-stable compounds, Wolff–Kishner for base-stable ones.

widgets.title: MPV reduction and Oppenauer oxidation
widgets.steps: MPV: aluminium isopropoxide, Al(OiPr)₃, coordinates the ketone oxygen through aluminium.;;A hydride transfers from the isopropoxide α-C–H to the carbonyl carbon through a six-membered cyclic transition state.;;The ketone becomes the alcohol and the isopropoxide becomes acetone, which is distilled off to drive the equilibrium.;;Oppenauer is the reverse: a secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone with excess acetone or another ketone as hydride acceptor. C=C bonds are untouched.

title: ^53\. Mechanism: LiAlH 4 reduction of an amide

widgets.title: LiAlH₄ reduction of an amide to an amine, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: hydride adds to the amide carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral aluminate intermediate.;;Step 2: the nitrogen lone pair pushes out the O–Al group (oxygen leaves as an aluminate), forming an iminium ion.;;Step 3: a second hydride adds to the iminium carbon.;;Result: C=O becomes CH₂, giving the amine with the same number of carbons. The oxygen is lost as an aluminate, not as an alcohol.

title: ^49\. Mechanism: the reduction ladder of nitrobenzene

widgets.title: Reduction of nitrobenzene in acid and in base
widgets.steps: Acidic medium (Sn/HCl or Fe/HCl): Ar–NO₂ → Ar–N=O (nitroso) → Ar–NHOH (hydroxylamine) → Ar–NH₂ (aniline).;;Each stage takes two electrons and two protons, so the full reduction takes six electrons and six protons.;;Neutral medium (Zn/NH₄Cl): the reaction stops at the hydroxylamine, Ar–NHOH.;;Alkaline medium (Zn/NaOH): nitroso and hydroxylamine intermediates condense, giving azoxybenzene, then azobenzene and hydrazobenzene.

widgets.title: Tollens' test, step by step
widgets.steps: Reagent: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ in alkaline solution (ammoniacal silver nitrate).;;Step 1: the aldehyde hydrate (RCH(OH)₂) is oxidised, losing two electrons.;;Step 2: each Ag⁺ gains one electron, so two Ag⁺ are reduced to metallic silver for each aldehyde.;;Result: a silver mirror forms and the aldehyde becomes the carboxylate. Ketones do not react (except α-hydroxy ketones).

widgets.title: Rosenmund reduction, step by step
widgets.steps: Reagent: H₂ over Pd on BaSO₄, poisoned with quinoline or sulfur.;;The acyl chloride adsorbs on the catalyst and hydrogenolysis replaces Cl with H, giving the aldehyde and HCl.;;The poison weakens the catalyst, so the aldehyde is not reduced further to the alcohol.;;Compare Stephen reduction: SnCl₂/HCl reduces a nitrile to an imine salt, which hydrolyses to the aldehyde.

widgets.title: Dakin oxidation, step by step
widgets.steps: Requirement: an o- or p-hydroxy aryl aldehyde or ketone, treated with H₂O₂ in base.;;Step 1: HOO⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral intermediate.;;Step 2: the aryl group migrates from carbon to oxygen as hydroxide leaves, forming an aryl formate (or ester).;;Step 3: hydrolysis gives the catechol or hydroquinone, with the carbon-chain carbonyl lost as formate or carboxylate.

widgets.title: Etard reaction, in outline
widgets.steps: Reagent: chromyl chloride, CrO₂Cl₂, in CS₂ or CCl₄ with a methylarene such as toluene.;;The CH₃ group forms a brown solid chromium complex (the Étard complex), and the oxidation stops at this stage.;;Hydrolysis of the complex with water gives the aldehyde.;;Result: ArCH₃ becomes ArCHO with no over-oxidation to the acid.

widgets.title: Reaction profile with one intermediate (schematic)
widgets.note: Schematic profile: heights are illustrative, not measured values.

widgets.title: Reading a reaction profile
widgets.steps: Peaks are transition states (highest-energy points, not isolable). Valleys between peaks are intermediates (real species with a finite lifetime).;;The step with the highest peak is the rate-determining step.;;The activation energy (Ea) is the gap from the reactants to the next peak; the overall ΔH is the gap from reactants to products.;;By the Hammond postulate, a step that forms an unstable intermediate has a late, product-like transition state.

widgets.title: Carbocation stability and rearrangement
widgets.steps: A carbocation is an sp² carbon with an empty p orbital and a +1 charge; it is planar, so a nucleophile can attack from either face.;;Stability order: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl, due to hyperconjugation and the +I effect of alkyl groups.;;Resonance helps more: allyl and benzyl cations are stabilised by delocalisation.;;A 1,2-hydride or 1,2-alkyl shift occurs when it gives a more stable cation (for example 2° → 3°), which explains rearranged products.

widgets.title: Carbanion stability
widgets.steps: A carbanion has a carbon with three bonds and a lone pair, usually sp³ and pyramidal (a delocalised carbanion is planar).;;Stability order for alkyl carbanions: methyl > 1° > 2° > 3°, the reverse of carbocations, because alkyl groups push electron density onto an already electron-rich carbon.;;Stabilising factors: more s character (sp > sp² > sp³), resonance (enolate, benzyl), and −I or −M groups.;;More stable carbanions come from more acidic C–H bonds.

widgets.title: Free-radical stability and chain reaction
widgets.steps: A radical has an unpaired electron on carbon, generated by homolysis with heat, light or an initiator.;;Stability order: benzyl ≈ allyl > 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl, matching the weakness of the C–H bond being broken.;;Radical reactions are chains: initiation creates radicals, propagation regenerates them, and termination removes two radicals together.;;Radicals do not rearrange by 1,2-hydride shifts as carbocations do.

widgets.title: Carbenes: singlet and triplet
widgets.steps: A carbene is a neutral divalent carbon with six valence electrons, such as :CH₂ or :CCl₂.;;Singlet carbene: paired electrons in one sp² orbital with an empty p orbital; it adds to alkenes in one concerted step with stereospecific syn addition.;;Triplet carbene: two unpaired electrons in different orbitals; it behaves like a diradical and adds non-stereospecifically.;;Generation: CHCl₃ + base gives :CCl₂; CH₂N₂ with heat or light gives :CH₂ with loss of N₂.

widgets.title: Nitrenes
widgets.steps: A nitrene is the nitrogen analogue of a carbene: a neutral, monovalent nitrogen with six valence electrons (R–N:).;;Generation: heating or photolysis of an azide R–N₃ expels N₂ and leaves R–N:.;;The Hofmann, Curtius and Lossen rearrangements are written either through a free nitrene or, more accurately, as a concerted migration with N₂ or halide loss.;;Nitrenes can insert into C–H bonds and add to alkenes to give aziridines.

widgets.title: Benzyne (elimination–addition), step by step
widgets.steps: Conditions: an unactivated aryl halide with a very strong base such as NaNH₂ in liquid NH₃.;;Step 1: the base removes a proton ortho to the halogen, and the halide leaves, giving benzyne with a strained 'triple bond' in the ring.;;Step 2: the nucleophile (NH₂⁻) adds to either carbon of the aryne, then the aryl anion is protonated.;;Result: with a substituted ring, the incoming group can end up on the carbon next to the original one (cine substitution), giving a mixture of isomers.

widgets.title: Bromine addition to an alkene, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: as Br₂ approaches, the alkene π electrons polarise the Br–Br bond; Br⁺ is transferred to the alkene, forming a cyclic bromonium ion and Br⁻.;;Step 2: Br⁻ attacks one carbon of the bromonium ion from the side opposite the bridging bromine (backside attack).;;Result: anti addition. Cyclohexene gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane. A cis alkene gives the racemic pair of one diastereomer, a trans alkene the other.;;In water the solvent attacks the bromonium ion instead, giving a bromohydrin (Markovnikov, anti).

widgets.title: Allylic bromination with NBS, step by step
widgets.steps: NBS supplies a very low, steady concentration of Br₂ (from HBr + NBS), so ionic addition to the C=C is suppressed.;;Initiation: light or a peroxide makes Br• radicals.;;Propagation 1: Br• removes an allylic hydrogen, giving a resonance-stabilised allyl radical and HBr.;;Propagation 2: the allyl radical takes Br from Br₂, giving the allyl bromide and a new Br•. An unsymmetrical allyl radical can give two isomeric bromides.

widgets.title: Cyclopropanation, step by step
widgets.steps: Simmons–Smith: CH₂I₂ with Zn(Cu) gives a zinc carbenoid, ICH₂ZnI, which transfers CH₂ to the alkene in one concerted step.;;Dichlorocarbene: CHCl₃ with a base gives :CCl₂, which adds to the alkene to give a 1,1-dichlorocyclopropane.;;Both additions are stereospecific and syn: a cis alkene gives a cis-substituted cyclopropane, and a trans alkene gives trans.

widgets.title: HBr addition to buta-1,3-diene: 1,2 versus 1,4
widgets.steps: Step 1: H⁺ adds to C-1, giving the resonance-stabilised allylic cation (positive charge shared by C-2 and C-4).;;Step 2: Br⁻ can attack C-2, giving the 1,2-adduct (3-bromobut-1-ene) quickly.;;Step 2 alternative: Br⁻ attacks C-4, giving the 1,4-adduct (1-bromobut-2-ene), which has the more substituted, more stable C=C.;;Low temperature gives mostly 1,2 (kinetic control); higher temperature gives mostly 1,4 (thermodynamic control, equilibrating products).

widgets.title: SNi with thionyl chloride, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the alcohol attacks SOCl₂, giving an alkyl chlorosulfite, R–O–S(=O)Cl, and HCl.;;Step 2: the C–O bond ionises and the chloride is delivered from the same face by the departing chlorosulfite, in an ion pair.;;Result: SO₂ escapes and the alkyl chloride forms with retention of configuration.;;With pyridine present, chloride attacks from the back (SN2) instead, and the product has inverted configuration.

widgets.title: Neighbouring-group participation, step by step
widgets.steps: Setup: a neighbouring group with a lone pair (such as SR, NR₂, Br or COO⁻) sits close to the leaving group.;;Step 1: the neighbouring group displaces the leaving group by an internal SN2 attack, forming a cyclic intermediate (inversion #1). The rate is higher than for an analogue with no such group.;;Step 2: the external nucleophile opens the ring from the back (inversion #2).;;Result: two inversions give overall retention of configuration, and the rate is enhanced.

widgets.title: E1cB elimination, step by step
widgets.steps: Requirement: an acidic β-hydrogen (next to C=O, NO₂ or CN) and a poor leaving group (such as OH or OR).;;Step 1: the base removes the acidic β-hydrogen, giving a stabilised carbanion (the conjugate base).;;Step 2 (slow): the carbanion expels the leaving group, forming the C=C.;;Example: the dehydration step of the aldol condensation. Compare E1 (leaving group first) and E2 (single concerted step).

widgets.title: SNAr (addition–elimination), step by step
widgets.steps: Requirement: electron-withdrawing groups (NO₂) ortho or para to the leaving group.;;Step 1 (slow): the nucleophile adds to the ring carbon bearing the halogen, giving the resonance-stabilised Meisenheimer complex.;;Step 2 (fast): the halide leaves and the aromatic ring re-forms.;;More nitro groups make the reaction faster; the order of leaving-group reactivity is F > Cl > Br > I.

widgets.title: Generating the electrophiles of EAS
widgets.steps: Nitration: HNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂NO₃⁺ → NO₂⁺ (nitronium ion) + H₂O.;;Sulfonation: fuming H₂SO₄ gives SO₃ as the electrophile (HSO₃⁺ in some descriptions). Sulfonation is reversible.;;Halogenation: Br₂ + FeBr₃ polarises Br–Br, so Br⁺ is transferred to the ring (Br–Br···FeBr₃).;;Friedel–Crafts: R–Cl + AlCl₃ gives R⁺ (or the polarised complex), and RCOCl + AlCl₃ gives the acylium ion RCO⁺.

widgets.title: Acetoacetic ester synthesis of a ketone, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: NaOEt removes an α-hydrogen between the two carbonyls (pKa ≈ 11), giving a stabilised enolate.;;Step 2: the enolate attacks a primary alkyl halide by SN2, giving the α-alkyl acetoacetic ester. A second alkylation is possible.;;Step 3: aqueous NaOH hydrolyses the ester to the β-keto acid.;;Step 4: on heating, the β-keto acid decarboxylates (loses CO₂) through a cyclic six-membered transition state, giving a methyl ketone R–CH₂–CO–CH₃.

widgets.title: Malonic ester synthesis of a carboxylic acid, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: NaOEt removes an α-hydrogen of diethyl malonate (pKa ≈ 13), giving a stabilised enolate.;;Step 2: the enolate is alkylated by a primary alkyl halide (SN2). Repeat for a dialkyl product.;;Step 3: hydrolysis (NaOH, then H₃O⁺) converts both esters to a malonic acid.;;Step 4: heating decarboxylates the substituted malonic acid, giving R–CH₂–COOH: the alkyl group R from R–X gains a CH₂COOH unit (two carbons).

widgets.title: Osazone formation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: phenylhydrazine condenses with the C-1 aldehyde to give a phenylhydrazone.;;Step 2: a second molecule of phenylhydrazine oxidises the C-2 CHOH to C=O, releasing aniline and NH₃.;;Step 3: a third molecule condenses with the new C-2 carbonyl, giving the osazone (three equivalents of phenylhydrazine in all).;;Result: C-1 and C-2 become identical in glucose, fructose and mannose, so they give the same osazone.

title: ^6\.4 Kiliani cyanohydrin step and the Strecker

widgets.title: Kiliani chain extension and Strecker amino acid synthesis
widgets.steps: Kiliani: cyanide adds to the aldehyde carbon of the sugar, giving a cyanohydrin and creating a new stereocentre (two epimers).;;Hydrolysis of the nitrile gives an aldonic acid (lactone); reduction then gives an aldose with one more carbon.;;Strecker: an aldehyde reacts with NH₃ to form an imine, which cyanide attacks, giving an α-aminonitrile.;;Hydrolysis of the nitrile gives the racemic α-amino acid.

widgets.title: DCC peptide coupling, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the carboxylic acid of the N-protected amino acid adds to one C=N of DCC, giving an O-acylisourea (an activated acyl derivative).;;Step 2: the amine of the second amino acid attacks the activated carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.;;Step 3: dicyclohexylurea (DCU) is expelled, leaving the new peptide (amide) bond.;;DCU is insoluble and filtered off. Protecting groups on the other amine and acid groups prevent unwanted couplings.

widgets.title: Edman degradation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: phenyl isothiocyanate (PhN=C=S) reacts with the free N-terminal amino group at mildly basic pH, giving a phenylthiocarbamoyl (PTC) peptide.;;Step 2: anhydrous acid cleaves the first peptide bond, releasing the N-terminal residue as a thiazolinone.;;Step 3: the thiazolinone is converted to the stable phenylthiohydantoin (PTH) amino acid and identified.;;The rest of the chain (one residue shorter) is left intact, so the cycle can be repeated.

widgets.title: Lobry de Bruyn–van Ekenstein transformation
widgets.steps: In dilute base, the α-hydrogen of an aldose (C-2) is removed, giving an enediolate (C-1=C-2 with O⁻).;;Protonation at C-2 re-forms either epimer; protonation at C-1 gives the ketose.;;Result: glucose, mannose and fructose interconvert through the common enediol.;;Because of this, fructose (a ketose) gives positive tests with Tollens' and Fehling's reagents, which look for aldehydes.

widgets.title: Why RNA is hydrolysed by base but DNA survives
widgets.steps: RNA has a 2′-OH group on ribose next to the phosphodiester linkage; DNA has no 2′-OH.;;Step 1: base deprotonates the 2′-OH, and the 2′-O⁻ attacks the adjacent phosphorus, forming a five-membered cyclic 2′,3′-phosphate and expelling the 5′-O of the next nucleotide (chain cleaved).;;Step 2: water opens the cyclic phosphate to give 2′- and 3′-phosphate monomers.;;DNA has no 2′-OH and so no intramolecular nucleophile; this is why DNA is stable and suitable for storing genetic information.

widgets.title: Chymotrypsin (serine protease), step by step
widgets.steps: Catalytic triad: Ser-195, His-57 and Asp-102. His acts as a general base and takes the proton from Ser-OH.;;Stage 1 (acylation): the Ser alkoxide attacks the peptide carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate (stabilised by the oxyanion hole); the C–N bond breaks, releasing the amine part and leaving an acyl-enzyme.;;Stage 2 (deacylation): water, activated by His, attacks the acyl-enzyme, forming a second tetrahedral intermediate.;;The Ser–acyl bond breaks, releasing the carboxylic acid half and regenerating the free enzyme.

widgets.title: Acid-catalysed ester hydrolysis (AAC2), step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: H⁺ protonates the carbonyl oxygen, making the carbon more electrophilic.;;Step 2: water attacks, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.;;Step 3: proton transfer converts the OR group into a good leaving group (ROH).;;Step 4: the alcohol leaves and the C=O re-forms; loss of H⁺ gives the carboxylic acid. Every step is reversible, so a large excess of water drives hydrolysis.

widgets.title: Step-growth polymerisation, step by step
widgets.steps: Monomers carry two functional groups (such as a diacid and a diamine); any two molecules can react, giving dimers, trimers and so on.;;Each coupling releases a small molecule (water, HCl), as in nylon-6,6 from adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine.;;Molar mass rises slowly. A high degree of polymerisation needs a conversion near 99% (Carothers equation: Xn = 1/(1 − p)).;;An exact 1:1 ratio of the functional groups is needed; an excess of one monomer limits chain length.

widgets.title: Fischer esterification, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the acid catalyst protonates the carbonyl oxygen of the carboxylic acid.;;Step 2: the alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral intermediate; proton transfer follows.;;Step 3: water leaves from the tetrahedral intermediate, and loss of H⁺ gives the ester.;;All steps are reversible; use excess alcohol or remove water to push the equilibrium toward the ester. Labelling shows the alkoxy oxygen comes from the alcohol and the acyl C–O(H) bond breaks.

widgets.title: Alcohol + HX, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: HX protonates the OH group, giving R–OH₂⁺.;;Tertiary and secondary (benzylic/allylic) alcohols: water leaves to give a carbocation (SN1), then X⁻ attacks. Rearrangement is possible.;;Primary alcohols: X⁻ attacks the protonated alcohol directly (SN2) with inversion at carbon.;;Reactivity of HX: HI > HBr > HCl; ZnCl₂ helps with HCl. Alcohol reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1° (SN1 path).

widgets.title: Lucas test, step by step
widgets.steps: Reagent: anhydrous ZnCl₂ in concentrated HCl. ZnCl₂ coordinates the alcohol oxygen, making OH a better leaving group.;;Tertiary alcohol: the carbocation forms at once and chloride adds; the insoluble alkyl chloride makes the solution turn cloudy immediately.;;Secondary alcohol: turbidity appears in about 5 minutes.;;Primary alcohol: no turbidity at room temperature (SN2 is slow). The test fails for alcohols with more than 6 carbons (not soluble in the reagent).

widgets.title: Pinacol rearrangement of a 1,2-diol, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: acid protonates one OH, and water leaves to give a carbocation (at the carbon giving the more stable cation).;;Step 2: a group on the neighbouring carbon (methyl, aryl, H) shifts to the cation (1,2-shift).;;Step 3: the oxygen lone pair stabilises the new cation, giving a protonated ketone.;;Step 4: loss of H⁺ gives the ketone (for pinacol, pinacolone, (CH₃)₃C–CO–CH₃).

widgets.title: Fries rearrangement, step by step
widgets.steps: Substrate: a phenolic ester (Ar–O–CO–R) with AlCl₃.;;Step 1: AlCl₃ complexes the carbonyl oxygen, and the acyl group is transferred to the ring as an acylium-type species (intermolecular or intimate ion pair).;;Step 2: electrophilic acylation of the activated ring at the ortho or para position, then work-up.;;Result: hydroxyaryl ketones. Low temperature favours para; high temperature favours ortho (chelated by Al, thermodynamic).

widgets.title: Aromatic Claisen rearrangement, step by step
widgets.steps: Substrate: allyl phenyl ether, heated to about 200 °C.;;Step 1: a concerted [3,3]-sigmatropic shift through a six-membered cyclic transition state moves the allyl group from O to the ortho carbon, with inversion of the allyl unit (the γ-carbon bonds to the ring).;;Step 2: the resulting cyclohexadienone tautomerises, restoring the aromatic ring and giving o-allylphenol.;;If both ortho positions are blocked, a second [3,3] shift (Cope) moves the allyl group to the para position.

widgets.title: Cleavage of an ether with HI, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: HI protonates the ether oxygen, giving an oxonium ion R–O⁺(H)–R′.;;Step 2 (primary/methyl groups): I⁻ attacks the less hindered carbon by SN2, giving R–I and R′–OH.;;With a tertiary group, the C–O bond ionises (SN1) and the tertiary iodide forms.;;Excess HI converts the alcohol to a second alkyl iodide. Aryl alkyl ethers give an alkyl iodide and phenol (the aryl C–O bond does not break).

widgets.title: Knoevenagel condensation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: a weak base (piperidine, pyridine) removes a proton from the active methylene compound (such as CH₂(CO₂Et)₂), giving a stabilised enolate.;;Step 2: the enolate adds to the aldehyde or ketone carbonyl carbon, giving a β-hydroxy intermediate.;;Step 3: dehydration (loss of H₂O) gives the α,β-unsaturated product.;;Doebner variant: with malonic acid in pyridine, decarboxylation follows, giving a cinnamic-type acid.

widgets.title: Mannich reaction, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: an amine (secondary) and formaldehyde condense to the iminium ion, CH₂=N⁺R₂.;;Step 2: the enol (or enolate) of a ketone with an α-hydrogen attacks the iminium ion at carbon.;;Result: a β-amino ketone (Mannich base), R–CO–CH₂–CH₂–NR₂.;;Heating the Mannich base can eliminate the amine, giving an α,β-unsaturated ketone.

widgets.title: Imine formation and the pH profile
widgets.steps: Step 1: the amine adds to the carbonyl carbon, giving a carbinolamine (tetrahedral intermediate).;;Step 2: acid protonates the OH group of the carbinolamine, and water leaves with the nitrogen lone pair, giving an iminium ion; loss of H⁺ gives the imine.;;pH profile: the rate is highest near pH 4 to 5. At lower pH the amine is protonated and not nucleophilic; at higher pH the OH is not protonated enough to leave.;;Reductive amination: NaBH₃CN or H₂/Ni then reduces the C=N to the amine.

widgets.title: Acylation of an amine by an acid chloride
widgets.steps: Step 1: the nitrogen lone pair attacks the acyl chloride carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral intermediate.;;Step 2: the C=O re-forms and Cl⁻ is expelled, giving the N-acylammonium ion.;;Step 3: a base (pyridine or a second equivalent of amine) removes H⁺, giving the amide.;;The amide N is much less basic and nucleophilic than the amine, so the reaction stops at the monoacylated product.

widgets.title: Curtius rearrangement, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: an acyl chloride and NaN₃ give the acyl azide, R–CO–N₃.;;Step 2: on heating, the R group migrates from carbon to nitrogen as N₂ leaves (concerted), forming the isocyanate R–N=C=O. R keeps its configuration.;;Step 3: water adds to the isocyanate, giving a carbamic acid, which loses CO₂ to give R–NH₂.;;Lossen: the same migration occurs from an O-acylated hydroxamic acid in base. Both give an amine with one carbon fewer than the acid.

widgets.title: Schotten–Baumann acylation
widgets.steps: Conditions: an acyl chloride with an amine, alcohol or phenol in the presence of aqueous NaOH (or pyridine).;;Step 1: the nucleophile (RNH₂, ROH or ArO⁻) attacks the acyl chloride's carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.;;Step 2: Cl⁻ leaves, forming the amide or ester.;;The base neutralises the HCl formed, which would otherwise protonate the amine and stop the reaction.

widgets.title: Favorskii rearrangement, step by step
widgets.steps: Substrate: an α-halo ketone that has an α′-hydrogen, with an alkoxide or hydroxide base.;;Step 1: the base removes the α′-hydrogen, forming an enolate.;;Step 2: the enolate displaces the halide intramolecularly, forming a strained cyclopropanone intermediate.;;Step 3: the nucleophile (RO⁻) adds to the cyclopropanone C=O, and the ring opens to the more stable carbanion; protonation gives the rearranged ester (or acid). A cyclic α-halo ketone undergoes ring contraction.

widgets.title: Cope rearrangement
widgets.steps: Substrate: a 1,5-diene (C=C–C–C–C=C).;;A concerted [3,3]-sigmatropic shift through a chair-like six-membered transition state breaks the central C3–C4 σ bond and makes a new C1–C6 σ bond.;;The equilibrium favours the more stable (more substituted or conjugated) diene.;;Oxy-Cope: a hydroxyl at C3 gives an enol, which tautomerises to a carbonyl compound, making the reaction irreversible.

widgets.title: Stork enamine alkylation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: a ketone and a secondary amine (such as pyrrolidine), with acid catalysis, give an enamine and water.;;Step 2: the enamine β-carbon (nucleophilic, from the nitrogen lone pair) attacks an alkyl halide or Michael acceptor, giving an iminium salt.;;Step 3: aqueous hydrolysis gives the α-alkylated ketone and regenerates the amine.;;Advantage over enolate chemistry: milder, and gives monoalkylation under neutral conditions.

widgets.title: Benzoin condensation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon of one benzaldehyde, giving a cyanohydrin alkoxide; proton transfer gives a carbanion stabilised by the nitrile (the acyl-anion equivalent).;;Step 2: this carbanion attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second benzaldehyde, forming a new C–C bond.;;Step 3: proton transfer and loss of cyanide regenerate the catalyst and give benzoin, PhCH(OH)–CO–Ph.;;Requirement: an aromatic aldehyde with no α-hydrogen. The cyanide ion reverses the polarity of the carbonyl carbon (umpolung).

widgets.title: Perkin reaction, step by step
widgets.steps: Reagents: an aromatic aldehyde, an acid anhydride with α-hydrogens (acetic anhydride) and its sodium salt (sodium acetate) as the base, heated.;;Step 1: acetate removes an α-hydrogen from the anhydride, giving an enolate.;;Step 2: the enolate adds to the aldehyde carbonyl, giving an alkoxide that becomes a β-acyloxy (mixed anhydride) intermediate.;;Step 3: elimination of acetic acid forms the C=C, and hydrolysis gives the α,β-unsaturated acid. Benzaldehyde gives cinnamic acid.

widgets.title: Robinson annulation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1 (Michael addition): the enolate of a ketone adds to the β-carbon of an α,β-unsaturated ketone such as methyl vinyl ketone, giving a 1,5-diketone.;;Step 2 (intramolecular aldol): an enolate formed from one ketone attacks the other carbonyl, closing a six-membered ring.;;Step 3 (dehydration): loss of water from the aldol gives a cyclohexenone.;;Result: a new six-membered ring fused onto the original ketone, the basis of steroid and terpene ring synthesis.

widgets.title: Hemiacetal and acetal formation, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: with acid, the carbonyl oxygen is protonated and the alcohol oxygen adds to the carbonyl carbon, giving a hemiacetal after loss of H⁺. Hemiacetals are usually not isolable for simple aldehydes.;;Step 2: acid protonates the hemiacetal OH, and water leaves, giving an oxocarbenium ion.;;Step 3: a second alcohol molecule adds to the oxocarbenium ion, and loss of H⁺ gives the acetal (a protecting group, stable to base).;;Intramolecularly, a hydroxy aldehyde (such as glucose) closes to a cyclic hemiacetal, which is why sugars exist mainly as rings.

widgets.title: Hinsberg test, step by step
widgets.steps: Reagent: benzenesulfonyl chloride, PhSO₂Cl, with aqueous NaOH.;;Primary amine: the nitrogen attacks sulfur, chloride leaves, giving PhSO₂NHR. This sulfonamide still has an N–H that NaOH removes, so it dissolves as a salt; acidification precipitates it.;;Secondary amine: gives PhSO₂NR₂, with no N–H, which is insoluble in alkali.;;Tertiary amine: no stable sulfonamide forms, so there is no reaction with the reagent.

widgets.title: Carbylamine (isocyanide) reaction, step by step
widgets.steps: Reagents: a primary amine, chloroform and KOH (only primary amines react).;;Step 1: hydroxide removes a proton from CHCl₃, which loses Cl⁻ to give dichlorocarbene, :CCl₂.;;Step 2: the amine nitrogen attacks the carbene carbon, and successive losses of HCl (with base) give the isocyanide, R–N⁺≡C⁻.;;Result: an isocyanide with a foul smell, used as a test for primary amines. Secondary and tertiary amines do not give it.

title: ^42\. Mechanism: the fate of the diazonium

widgets.title: Reactions of an arenediazonium ion
widgets.steps: Sandmeyer: Cu(I)Cl, CuBr or CuCN replaces N₂⁺ by Cl, Br or CN, by a radical process on copper.;;Balz–Schiemann: the tetrafluoroborate salt, ArN₂⁺BF₄⁻, is heated, giving ArF, N₂ and BF₃.;;Hydrolysis: warming the aqueous diazonium salt gives the phenol (aryl cation captured by water).;;Reduction: H₃PO₂ replaces N₂⁺ by H, which allows an amino group to be used as a temporary directing group.

widgets.title: Kolbe electrolysis, step by step
widgets.steps: A concentrated aqueous solution of a sodium carboxylate is electrolysed.;;Anode: the carboxylate gives up an electron and loses CO₂, giving an alkyl radical (RCOO⁻ → RCOO• → R• + CO₂).;;Two alkyl radicals combine, giving the alkane R–R with twice the carbons of R.;;Cathode: water is reduced, giving H₂ and OH⁻. A mixture of two carboxylates gives a statistical mixture of R–R, R–R′ and R′–R′.

widgets.title: Hunsdiecker reaction, step by step
widgets.steps: Step 1: the silver salt of the carboxylic acid reacts with bromine to give an acyl hypobromite, RCOO–Br.;;Step 2: homolysis of the weak O–Br bond gives a carboxyl radical, RCOO•, and Br•.;;Step 3: the carboxyl radical loses CO₂, giving R•, which takes Br from another acyl hypobromite (chain propagation).;;Result: an alkyl bromide with one carbon fewer than the acid.

widgets.title: Gattermann–Koch formylation, step by step
widgets.steps: Reagents: CO, HCl and AlCl₃ with CuCl, on a benzene ring.;;Step 1: CO and HCl with the Lewis acid generate the formyl cation, HC≡O⁺, the electrophile.;;Step 2: the arene attacks the formyl cation, giving the arenium ion; loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity.;;Result: an aryl aldehyde (benzene gives benzaldehyde). The method fails for phenols and amines, which complex the Lewis acid.

widgets.title: Dieckmann condensation, step by step
widgets.steps: Substrate: a diester such as diethyl hexanedioate, with NaOEt.;;Step 1: ethoxide removes an α-hydrogen from one ester, giving an enolate.;;Step 2: the enolate attacks the other ester carbonyl intramolecularly, forming a ring and expelling ethoxide: a cyclic β-keto ester.;;Step 3: the β-keto ester is deprotonated by base, which drives the equilibrium; acid work-up gives the cyclic product. 1,6-diesters give five-membered rings and 1,7-diesters give six-membered rings.

widgets.title: Pinacol coupling, step by step
widgets.steps: Reagent: magnesium amalgam (or Mg or Zn), with a ketone such as acetone.;;Step 1: the metal transfers an electron to the carbonyl, forming a ketyl radical anion.;;Step 2: two ketyl radicals combine at carbon, forming the C–C bond.;;Step 3: protonation gives the 1,2-diol (pinacol, 2,3-dimethylbutane-2,3-diol). Acid then converts it by the pinacol rearrangement to pinacolone.
